name: Boom Bap
story: The crunchy, sampled drum break of 1990s New York hip-hop — DJ Premier, Pete Rock, and the SP-1200. Kick, snare, and swung sixteenths on a chopped loop.

name: Four on the Floor
story: Every 909 house record ever — four straight kicks, offbeat hats, clap on 2 and 4. The metronome-to-club pipeline in one bar.

name: Standard Rock Beat
story: Eighth-note hats, kick on 1 and the "and of 3," snare on 2 and 4. The backbeat that holds up half of Western popular music.

name: Anthemic Rock
story: Slow, punishing backbeat with a crash on one — Queen, Zeppelin, U2. The grammar of the stadium singalong.

name: Pop Clap Beat
story: Four-on-the-floor kick, clap on 2 and 4 — the default grid of modern radio pop from Max Martin to Dua Lipa.

name: Classic Disco
story: Four-on-the-floor kick with pumping offbeat open hats — the sound of Studio 54, the Bee Gees, and the grandparent of every modern dance beat.

name: Train Beat
story: Constant eighth-note snare with accents on 2 and 4, mimicking a freight train rolling over rails. Johnny Cash built a career on top of it.

name: Country Two-Step
story: Honky-tonk dance floor pulse — four on the floor with a backbeat and nothing fancy. Built for boots sliding in unison.

name: Pop Punk
story: Chopping eighth hats, a sprint-tempo backbeat, and kicks snaking between guitar accents — Green Day, Blink-182, the mall in 2002.

name: Double Bass Metal
story: Sixteenth notes on two kick pedals, snare on the backbeat. The engine of thrash, death, and every Iron Maiden gallop since 1980.

name: Funky Drummer
story: Clyde Stubblefield's 1970 two-bar break for James Brown — the most sampled rhythm in recorded history. Ghost-note lace between the main hits carries the groove.

name: Cissy Strut
story: Zigaboo Modeliste with the Meters — New Orleans funk built out of negative space. Every gap is as composed as every hit.

name: New Orleans Second Line
story: The syncopated parade rhythm that follows New Orleans brass bands down the street — African and Caribbean accents filtered through a marching drum tradition.

name: P-Funk Groove
story: George Clinton's Mothership rhythm — dense hat subdivisions, open-hat punctuation, kicks weaving around the groove. Afrofuturism in a drum pattern.

name: Classic R&B
story: The slow-burn backbeat that carries soul, Motown chart sides, and quiet-storm radio from the 1960s onward.

name: Neo-Soul Dilla Feel
story: J Dilla's signature — kick and snare pushed and dragged off the grid so the beat limps with a human wobble. Questlove built Voodoo around it.

name: Neo-Soul Ghost Groove
story: Ghost notes carpet the space between backbeats — D'Angelo, Erykah Badu, the Soulquarians crew turning funk into a whispered conversation.

name: Motown Beat
story: Benny Benjamin and the Funk Brothers: four-on-the-floor kick with handclaps and tambourine riding the backbeat. The sound of Hitsville U.S.A.

name: One Drop
story: Carlton Barrett with Bob Marley & the Wailers. Beat 1 is empty — kick and rim shot both land on beat 3, and the bass plays the ghost of the downbeat.

name: Rockers
story: Sly Dunbar's answer to one-drop — steady quarter-note kick pulls the groove forward like a march while the snare keeps the reggae accent on beat 3.

name: Steppers
story: Four-on-the-floor reggae — the militant, marching style of Burning Spear and Black Uhuru. A Rastafarian drumbeat dressed in dub clothing.

name: Classic Ska Offbeat
story: The offbeat "upstroke" — hi-hats and guitar stab only on the ands. The pre-reggae sound of Kingston dances in the independence era.

name: Trap
story: Half-time feel at 140 — snare on beat 3 only, 808 sub-kick booming, skittering hi-hats. The Atlanta template that swallowed pop radio in the 2010s.

name: Trap Triplet Hats
story: Hi-hat triplet rolls fired before beats 2 and 4 — Lex Luger, Metro Boomin, the stuttering detail that made trap drums feel alive.

name: Lo-Fi Hip-Hop
story: Tape-saturated, swung, and deliberately imperfect — the Nujabes-to-YouTube-radio pipeline that made hip-hop drums into study music.

name: UK Drill
story: South London by way of Chicago — sliding 808 bass, off-kilter kicks, and snare rolls. Drill's syncopation rewrote the hip-hop rulebook in the late 2010s.

name: Phonk
story: Memphis underground cassette rap looped through the internet and turned into drift-race music. Cowbell on the ands, 808s everywhere.

name: Jersey Club Bounce
story: Newark club dance music — triplet kick burst ("bed-squeak") detonating on the ands, quintuplet chants on the breaks. Pure choreographed chaos.

name: Classic House
story: Frankie Knuckles at the Warehouse — the stripped-down Roland-909 grid that built Chicago house and defined dance music worldwide.

name: Deep House
story: Shaker-soft sixteenths under a four-on-the-floor groove. The Larry Heard / Masters at Work lineage — house music with soul.

name: Acid House
story: Phuture's "Acid Tracks" — house drums under a snaking TB-303. The accidental bass synth that sparked the UK rave scene.

name: Detroit Techno
story: Juan Atkins, Derrick May, Kevin Saunderson — "Strings of Life," "Big Fun." Detroit techno as Black futurism at the end of Motown.

name: Berlin Techno
story: Post-Wall warehouse techno — driving straight hats under an unrelenting kick. Tresor, Berghain, the sound of the tunnel.

name: Minimal Techno
story: Villalobos, Hawtin, Kompakt — techno stripped back to a kick, a rim, and a click. The DJ builds the record.

name: UK Garage 2-Step
story: The 2-step: garage with the kick skipping beat 3, snare still on 2 and 4. Add heavy swing and you've got MJ Cole and Todd Edwards on a UK pirate station.

name: Classic Dubstep
story: 140 BPM with a half-time snare on beat 3 — the South London template behind Skream, Benga, and every wobble bass on earth.

name: Amen Break
story: Gregory Coleman's six-second drum break on The Winstons' "Amen, Brother" (1969). Chopped, pitched, and relooped, it became the DNA of jungle, DnB, and half of UK electronic music.

name: Jungle Break
story: UK hardcore sped up, dubwise bass dropped in, Amen breaks chopped to ribbons. The 1992–95 pirate radio sound that birthed DnB.

name: Medium Jazz Swing
story: The spang-a-lang ride pattern, hat comping on 2 and 4, feathered bass drum. The backbone of every standard played after 1940.

name: Bebop Fast Ride
story: Max Roach, Kenny Clarke — the bebop reinvention of time. Ride cymbal carries the swing pulse and the bass drum drops bombs.

name: Jazz Waltz
story: Ride pattern stretched over three beats. "My Favorite Things," "Bluesette," "Someday My Prince Will Come" — the jazz triple meter.

name: Purdie Shuffle
story: Bernard Purdie's half-time triplet shuffle — "Babylon Sisters," "Home at Last." Ghost-note lace between backbeats, the holy grail of feel.

name: Bossa Nova
story: Samba miniaturized for apartment music — Jobim, João Gilberto. Cross-stick clave on top, feathered kick below, hats whispering sixteenths.

name: Afrobeat (Tony Allen)
story: Tony Allen: "without Tony Allen, there would be no Afrobeat." Four limbs acting as four players — Fela Kuti's Africa 70 engine room.

name: Modern Afrobeats
story: Wizkid, Burna Boy, Davido — Lagos pop built on kick bounce, skipping hi-hats, and a layer of handclaps. Global radio since the late 2010s.

name: Amapiano
story: Johannesburg deep house mutated into a bass-heavy sub-genre — shuffling shaker, percussive log drum, and a tempo built for slow-dance soweto.

name: Gqom
story: Durban warehouse music — broken kick patterns, cavernous sub, percussive gqom ("drum" in isiZulu) clusters. Taxi-rank rhythm turned global.

name: Footwork
story: DJ Rashad, Traxman — 160 BPM syncopated triplets and broken kicks built for competitive dance battles on the South Side of Chicago.

name: Classic Trance
story: Frankfurt and Ibiza — four-on-the-floor under supersaw pads, built for hands-in-the-air moments. Paul van Dyk, Tiësto, Armin.

name: Country Two-Step (modern 4-on-floor)
story: The traditional Bob Wills honky-tonk shuffle (see country-two-step) has kick on beats 1 and 3. From about the mid-2000s onward, Nashville production moved the kick to four-on-the-floor so country singles could translate to dance floors and pop radio — the boom-chick became a thump-thump-thump-thump with the snare riding above.

name: Blues Shuffle
story: The 'ding-a ding-a' ride — hi-hat on the first and third of every triplet, kick on beats 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. Muddy Waters, B.B. King, Buddy Guy, SRV all built their grooves on this skeleton. The triplet feel is EXPLICIT in 12/8 — four dotted-quarter beats, each subdivided into three eighths. No swing slider needed; the microtiming is in the notation itself.

name: Shuffle Rock (rockabilly)
story: Chuck Berry, Jerry Lee Lewis, early Elvis. Same triplet subdivision as blues-shuffle, but the hi-hat doesn't spell out the shuffle — it just marks the dotted-quarter pulse. The triplet feel lives under the surface, giving rockabilly its rolling gallop without the explicit 'ding-a ding-a' of Chicago blues.

name: Half-Time Shuffle (Purdie/Porcaro)
story: Bernard Purdie's 'Babylon Sisters' groove, Jeff Porcaro's 'Rosanna' groove — two of the most imitated drum patterns in R&B and soft rock. The shuffle is there (triplet subdivisions, ghosted hi-hat), but the snare hits only on beat 3 instead of 2 and 4. That halving of the backbeat is why it feels so deep — the rhythm breathes twice as slowly while the hi-hat stays busy underneath.
